note: Authored guided breakdowns, eleven parts each, for the highest-frequency issues in observed.json. The judgement layer is written by the author; quotes come from observed.json and policy facts from faq.json and rules.json. Depths: agent handles it, specialist owns the edge cases, lead fixes the system that creates it. Each breakdown also carries four call panels that sit between the parts on the six call steps: callReady {open[], know[]}, callCheckpoint {confirm[], lines[]}, callAdvice {ask[], options[{do, why}], notNow} and callClose {recap[], lines[]}. Not an official bank source; confirm every figure in your systems.

breakdowns.title: Declined on a routine purchase after a fraud flag
breakdowns.surfaceRequest: "Why was my card declined? Make it work." Often with the amount and the place: "$60 for a pizza", "the locksmith to get back into my own home".
breakdowns.underlyingJob: Finish an ordinary purchase right now, often time-critical, and not be embarrassed in front of someone again tomorrow. The job is continuity of daily life, not a card.
breakdowns.emotionalRead: Anger on the surface, embarrassment underneath. Tell: the caller leads with the public setting (the queue, the counter, the kids) and the length of the wait. Repeating the amount means they feel the stakes were trivial and the humiliation disproportionate.
breakdowns.psychologicalNeeds: Competence and dignity (I was made to look like someone who cannot pay), control (a machine decided about my money), fairness (I did nothing wrong). Safety is low here unless the flag was for a real unknown charge.
riskFlags: Unanswered fraud alert: the restriction may be protecting a real compromise, so confirm the flagged transaction before lifting
Stale contact number on file, which is why the alert never landed
Client 60+: pace, callback offer, no product talk
Repeated declines over days signal a system or rules problem, not a client problem
breakdowns.engage: Name the place, the purchase and the wait in the first sentence, then give a time-boxed next step: "Declined at the pharmacy for the prescription, and you have already waited. I can see the restriction and I can deal with it on this call; give me ninety seconds to confirm two things."
diagnose: Was the transaction the system flagged yours? (yes: lift and confirm the merchant can re-run; no: block, report, replacement)
Is the number we have for alerts the phone in your hand? (fix the cause of the silent alert)
Do you need this purchase to go through in the next ten minutes, and is there a second card or a wallet? (solve tonight while the restriction clears)
breakdowns.resolve: If the flagged item is theirs: verify, lift the restriction, tell them the decline will not repeat for that merchant, update the contact number, explain how to reply to the next alert. If not theirs: block, report, state liability (nothing after the report; $50 cap by law before it, bank proves negligence), temporary credit per policy, replacement 7 to 10 business days or emergency in 3, wallet for the gap. Either way: written confirmation before the call ends.

sayThisNotThis.say: "I can see exactly why it declined, and it is fixable on this call."
sayThisNotThis.not: "Our fraud team has placed a restriction on your card."
sayThisNotThis.why: Ownership and a path, versus a wall with no owner.

sayThisNotThis.say: "The alert at 10:38 did not reach you because the number we have ends in 0412; let me fix that now."
sayThisNotThis.not: "You should have replied to the text."

sayThisNotThis.say: "If you want to buy the medication in the next few minutes while this clears, here is what will work."
sayThisNotThis.not: "You would need to visit a branch."
sayThisNotThis.why: Solves tonight; the branch is the most-cited failure in the corpus.

breakdowns.afterCall: Note: restriction lifted after client confirmed [merchant] transaction, contact number updated, alert preferences confirmed, written confirmation sent. If fraud: claim reference, block time, replacement type ordered, wallet set up, client told the figures in writing.
breakdowns.preventAndFeedBack: Volume driver: alerts sent to stale numbers. Lead action: report declines-after-unanswered-alert as a root cause; propose a prompt to confirm the mobile number at every verified contact, and an IVR message during the restriction that routes straight to the desk that can lift it.

open: The card's status and the restriction: when it was placed and which purchase set it off
The last few authorisations, so you can read the declined purchase back to them
The alert history: what was sent, to which number, and whether anyone replied
The contact details on file, to compare with the phone they are calling from
know: A fraud flag protects the client. Confirm the flagged purchase is theirs before you lift anything.
The usual cause is an alert that went to an old number. Find that out early. It is the fix that stops the next decline.
They are often still at the counter. In the first minute, speed matters more than explanation.
If the flagged purchase is not theirs, this becomes a fraud call: block, report, replace. The liability figures are in Policy for this issue. Confirm in your systems before you quote one.

confirm: Tell them the restriction is off and that the same merchant can run the card again
If they are still at the till, stay on the line while they try it
Read back the number the alerts now go to
lines: "The restriction is off and the pharmacy can run the card again now. Do you want to try it while I stay on the line?"
"Is the decline the only thing that went wrong today, or is there anything else about the card that is worrying you?"

ask: "Is the mobile number we have the one you carry?"
"When we text you about a purchase, do you usually reply?"
"Do you have another way to pay if the card is ever stopped again?"

options.do: Update the alert number
options.why: The next alert reaches them and they clear it with one reply. The trade-off: it has to be changed again if they change phones.

options.do: Add the card to their phone wallet
options.why: A backup if the plastic is declined or lost. The trade-off: it only works where tap is accepted.

options.do: Show the lock in the app
options.why: Instant if the card is misplaced. The trade-off: a lock is not a report, so a lost or stolen card still needs a call.

callAdvice.notNow: Limit increases, balance protection or any product while they are upset or in a fraud claim.

recap: Why it declined, in one plain sentence, without blame
What you changed: the restriction is off and the alert number is current
How to answer the next alert: reply to the text, and never give a code or a PIN to anyone who calls
The written confirmation they will receive
lines: "To recap: the card was stopped because our text about the pharmacy purchase went to an old number. I have lifted the restriction, and the alerts now go to the phone in your hand."
"If we text you about a purchase again, a one-word reply clears it. We will never ask you for a code or your PIN."
"Is there anything else I can help you with today? Thank you for bearing with me. I hope the rest of your day goes better than the checkout did."

depths.agent: Confirm the flagged transaction, lift or block, fix the number, solve tonight, confirm in writing.
depths.specialist: Recognise the rules pattern behind repeat declines (same merchant on consecutive days, limits that do not match the flag) and raise it with fraud strategy instead of lifting it a third time.
depths.lead: Measure declines-after-unanswered-alert as a share of all fraud restrictions; it is a contact-rate driver you can cut without touching the fraud model.

breakdowns.title: Locked or declined abroad, cannot reach anyone
breakdowns.surfaceRequest: "Unlock my card. I am in [country] and it is the only one I have." Often after hours on hold across time zones and at least one transfer.
breakdowns.underlyingJob: Pay for accommodation, food or transport tonight with no fallback, and regain control of the account without flying home. Secondary job: not be treated as a suspect for using their own money abroad.
breakdowns.emotionalRead: Fear first (stranded, often with family), anger second once the hold time is mentioned. Tell: the caller gives their location and the time there, and lists what they cannot do (no branch, mobile banking also locked). Resignation appears on repeat calls: "I know there's nothing you can do."
breakdowns.psychologicalNeeds: Safety (I am far from home and the money is gone), control (every door is locked), being believed (I told you I was travelling).
riskFlags: Mobile banking also locked means self-serve unlock is unavailable; do not send them to the app
Genuine compromise abroad is possible: verify the flagged items before lifting
Hotel and car-rental pre-authorisations can look like duplicate charges
Collect and global toll-free numbers exist; give them in writing for the next time
breakdowns.engage: "You are in Lisbon, the card declined at the hotel, and you cannot get to a branch. I can see the restriction and I can deal with it on this call. Give me ninety seconds, and before we hang up you will either have a working card or know exactly what will work instead."
diagnose: Which transaction triggered this, and was it yours?
Is mobile banking working, or locked too?
What do you need to pay for in the next 24 hours, and with what else could you pay it?
Which number can we reach you on where you are?
breakdowns.resolve: Verify fully, confirm the flagged items, lift the restriction and the mobile-banking lock if both are clean; tell them the merchant can re-run. If the items are not theirs: block, report, liability stated, emergency replacement in 3 business days or less to where they are, digital wallet set up now if the card can be re-added, and the collect number for the fraud desk. Explain that travel notification is no longer required but current contact details are what keep the card alive abroad.

sayThisNotThis.say: "I can lift this now and the hotel can run the card again in a few minutes."
sayThisNotThis.not: "You would need to visit a branch with two pieces of ID."
sayThisNotThis.why: The branch answer to someone abroad is the single most quoted failure.

sayThisNotThis.say: "Here is the number that works from Portugal, and I am putting it in a message to you now."
sayThisNotThis.not: "Call us back if it happens again."
sayThisNotThis.why: The loop is the complaint; the number in writing ends it.

sayThisNotThis.say: "The system could not reach you to check the transaction; that is why it stopped the card."
sayThisNotThis.why: Explains the mechanism without making them the suspect.

breakdowns.afterCall: Note: restriction and mobile lock lifted after verification of [items]; contact number abroad recorded; collect number sent in writing; emergency card ordered to [city] if applicable; client told wallet route.
breakdowns.preventAndFeedBack: Driver: restrictions placed while the client is unreachable abroad, with the self-serve path (the app) locked by the same event. Lead action: separate the card restriction from the mobile-banking lock in the rules where possible, and surface the global toll-free number in the decline message.

open: The card's status and the restriction, and whether mobile banking is locked as well
Recent foreign authorisations, including hotel and car-rental holds
The contact details on file, and a number that reaches them where they are
The emergency replacement option and the phone numbers that work from outside Canada (Policy for this issue). Confirm in your systems.
know: They may have nothing else to pay with tonight. Solve tonight first, explain second.
Do not send them to a branch, and do not send them to the app if the app is locked too.
A real compromise abroad is possible. Verify the flagged purchases before you lift anything.
Verification feels like suspicion to someone stranded. Frame it as protection: "I am going to confirm it is you, so nobody else can unlock this card from another country."
Hotel and car-rental holds can look like double charges. A hold drops off when the merchant settles.

confirm: Tell them the card is unlocked and when the merchant can run it again
If mobile banking was locked, confirm they can sign in before you hang up
If the card had to be replaced, confirm where the emergency card is going, by when, and what they will pay with until then
lines: "The card is unlocked. Can the hotel try it again while I stay on the line?"
"Are you covered for tonight and tomorrow, or is there a payment I should know about before we hang up?"

ask: "How much longer are you away, and which countries are still ahead?"
"Which number can we reach you on while you travel?"
"Is this the only card you have with you?"

options.do: Put a reachable number on file for the trip
options.why: An alert they can answer keeps the card working. The trade-off: texts can be slow or cost money when roaming, so they should know to expect them.

options.do: Send the number that works from abroad in writing
options.why: Next time they skip the general queue. The trade-off: none for them, one minute for you.

options.do: Add the card to their phone wallet
options.why: A second way to pay if the plastic is lost or kept by a machine. The trade-off: it only works where tap is accepted.

options.do: Talk through a backup for the rest of the trip
options.why: A second card they already hold, or some local cash, means one stopped card no longer strands them. The trade-off: one more thing to keep safe.

callAdvice.notNow: A second card, a limit increase, travel insurance or any other product while they are stranded. If they raise one themselves, note it and offer a callback once they are home.

recap: What stopped the card and what you did about it
What will work tonight
The number that works from where they are, sent in writing
If a replacement is on the way: where it is going, by when, and what to do if it does not arrive
lines: "To recap: the card was stopped because we could not reach you to check a purchase. It is unlocked now and the hotel can run it again."
"I am sending you the number that works from where you are, so you do not have to sit in the general queue from abroad again."
"Is there anything else I can sort out before you go? Enjoy the rest of your trip."

depths.agent: Verify, lift or replace, solve tonight, give the working number in writing.
depths.specialist: Own the abroad queue: know which restrictions can be lifted by phone and which cannot, and get the emergency-card logistics right for the country.
depths.lead: Report abroad-locked calls by country and hour; the hold times in this cluster are a staffing and routing problem, not an agent problem.

breakdowns.title: Unauthorised charges; refund slow, partial or refused
breakdowns.surfaceRequest: "Someone used my card. I want it reversed and I want to know how this happened." Sometimes: "I locked it and a charge still went through."
breakdowns.underlyingJob: Get the money back, be certain it has stopped, and not be treated as the suspect. For debit clients the job includes rent or groceries this week.
breakdowns.emotionalRead: Fear that money is gone, quickly turning to anger if any sentence implies doubt. Tell: "EVEN AFTER LOCKING" in capitals, or the phrase "they implied it was my fault". Resignation on second contact.
breakdowns.psychologicalNeeds: Safety and being believed above all. Control (I did the right thing, I locked it, and it still happened).
riskFlags: Not everything the client lists is fraud: free-trial conversions, pre-authorisation holds and recurring payments are disputes or explanations
A lock does not stop pre-authorised payments; the client may think the bank failed
PIN used is never, alone, grounds to deny (Bank Act s. 627.33(3), FCAC B-6)
Debit: 10-business-day response rule; loss capped at the card's limits if the client contributed; the bank must prove contribution
After any migration, credits must follow to the new account
breakdowns.engage: "Charges you did not make, and a lock that did not stop one of them. First, I am blocking the card now so nothing further goes through, and nothing from this report onward can be charged to you. Then we go through the list together."
diagnose: For each item: did you or anyone authorised make it, or sign up for something that converts to paid?
When did you first notice, and when did you lock?
Has anyone else had the card, the PIN or your phone?
Is this debit or credit? (different rules and timelines)
breakdowns.resolve: Split the list into fraud, merchant dispute and hold, and say which is which. Fraud: block, report, claim per item, temporary credit per policy, update within the bank's stated days, replacement with the emergency option, liability stated. Dispute: merchant first with the evidence to gather, 120-day window. Hold: explain settlement. Explain in one sentence what a lock stops and what it lets through, as design, not failure. Confirm everything in writing with dates.

sayThisNotThis.say: "Nothing after this report can be charged to you, and for what already happened the law caps it at fifty dollars at most; in practice it is usually nothing, and the bank would have to prove you were grossly careless."
sayThisNotThis.not: "We will investigate and let you know if you are liable."
sayThisNotThis.why: The first states the actual rule; the second reads as a threat.

sayThisNotThis.say: "A lock stops purchases and cash; it is designed to let your bills keep paying, which is why that one went through. That does not make it yours to pay."
sayThisNotThis.not: "The lock only applies to certain transaction types."
sayThisNotThis.why: Explains design and removes the implied blame.

sayThisNotThis.say: "Two of the three on your list are fraud. The $14.99 is a trial that converted; that one we handle differently and I will tell you how."
sayThisNotThis.why: Disputing an authorised charge as fraud reverses later and produces a worse call.

breakdowns.afterCall: Note per item: classification, claim reference, block time, temporary credit status, replacement type, what the client was told about liability and timing, written confirmation sent. Debit: date of report for the 10-day clock.
breakdowns.preventAndFeedBack: Drivers: the lock's design is not explained in the app; alerts unanswered; trial conversions reported as fraud. Lead action: an in-app line under the lock toggle ("bills and subscriptions keep paying"); a claim-intake script that asks the trial question before classifying.

open: The transaction list, with each item's date, merchant and status: authorised or posted
The card's status: locked, blocked or open, and when that changed
Any open claim, temporary credit or earlier report on the file
Whether this is debit or credit. The rules and timelines differ (Policy for this issue). Confirm in your systems.
know: Block first, then talk. Nothing after the report can be charged to them.
Not every item on their list is fraud. A trial that turned into a paid plan, a hold and a recurring payment are each handled differently.
A lock stops purchases and cash. It lets bills keep paying, by design.
A PIN having been used is never, on its own, a reason to refuse a claim.
Never ask for a one-time code, and tell them nobody from the bank ever will.
No sentence should sound like doubt. They need to be believed before they can answer questions.

confirm: Read the list back: which items are fraud, which are a merchant dispute, which are a hold
Confirm the card is blocked and that nothing after the report is theirs to pay
Give the claim reference and say when they will next hear from the bank. Confirm the timing in your systems.
lines: "The card is blocked and I have reported the two charges you did not make. Does that match what you see on your side?"
"Is there any other charge, on this card or another one, that you are unsure about?"

ask: "Has anyone called or texted you lately asking for a code, a password or your card details?"
"Which bills or subscriptions are paid from this card?"
"Do you get a message when the card is used?"

options.do: Turn on transaction alerts
options.why: They see a charge within minutes and can call at once. The trade-off: more messages, and each one needs a glance.

options.do: List the bills on the old card number
options.why: They know which ones to move to the new card before a payment bounces. The trade-off: ten minutes of their time this week.

options.do: Change the passwords where the card number was saved
options.why: It closes the most likely leak. The trade-off: effort, and only they can do it.

options.do: Explain what a lock does and does not stop
options.why: Next time they lock the card and call as well. The trade-off: none, it takes one sentence.

callAdvice.notNow: Any product, limit change or balance protection. This is a fraud claim: no offers, even if the account shows one.

recap: Each item and what it is: fraud, dispute or hold
The card is blocked, and when the new one arrives, standard or emergency
The claim reference and when they will hear next
What they can be charged for the fraud items. State the rule from Policy for this issue, and confirm in your systems.
All of the above in writing
lines: "To recap: two charges reported as fraud under reference [reference], the card is blocked, and a new one is on its way. The third charge is a trial that renewed, and I have told you how we handle that one."
"Nothing after this report can be charged to you. You will have all of this in writing today."
"You did the right thing by calling. Is there anything else I can do for you today?"

depths.agent: Block, state liability correctly, classify each item, give figures in writing.
depths.specialist: Handle the contested cases: the client who shared a PIN under coercion, the affidavit, the Debit Code burden of proof, the migration that lost a credit.
depths.lead: Track claims denied on 'PIN used' alone; each one is a B-6 exposure. Report trial-conversion 'fraud' claims as a self-service gap.

breakdowns.title: Fraud alert received, cannot reach the fraud line, transferred in loops
breakdowns.surfaceRequest: "You texted me about a charge and now I cannot get through to anyone." Or: "I've been passed from one person to the next."
breakdowns.underlyingJob: Answer the bank's own question and get back to their day; make sure the charge is stopped if it is not theirs.
breakdowns.emotionalRead: Anxiety (the bank thinks something is wrong) turning to resentment (the bank made it my problem to reach them). Tell: the caller counts the transfers and the minutes.
breakdowns.psychologicalNeeds: Control (I responded, now respond to me), fairness (you contacted me), competence (I know how to answer a text, your system does not let me).
riskFlags: Alert may be the scam itself: real bank alerts never ask for links or personal information; a 'reply with your PIN' is not from the bank
Transfer again and the complaint is written; this call must be the one that ends the loop
If the charge is the client's, the restriction can be lifted here
breakdowns.engage: "You got our alert, you tried to answer it, and you have been passed around. I am sorry about that; you are with the right desk now and this call is where it gets handled. Let me look at the transaction the alert was about."
diagnose: Which transaction was the alert for, and is it yours?
Did the alert ask you for anything (a link, a code, your PIN)? (scam check)
Is the card restricted now, and do you need it in the next hour?
breakdowns.resolve: Confirm or deny with the client; lift the restriction or block and report; explain how the short-code alerts work and how to reply to the next one; set alert preferences to the number in their hand. If anyone asked for a code or PIN, treat it as a scam, protect the account, route to fraud. Written confirmation.

sayThisNotThis.say: "This is the desk that can act on that alert; nobody else needs to be involved."
sayThisNotThis.not: "Let me transfer you to the fraud department."
sayThisNotThis.why: The next transfer is the complaint.

sayThisNotThis.say: "Our alerts come from the short code and only ask you to reply yes or no. If any message asks for a link or a code, it is not us."
sayThisNotThis.not: "You should always respond to fraud alerts."
sayThisNotThis.why: Teaches the real tell, which protects them next time.

breakdowns.afterCall: Note: alert reference, client's confirm or deny, action taken, alert number updated, scam check result.
breakdowns.preventAndFeedBack: Driver: alert replies that go nowhere, and routing that sends alert callers to a general queue. Lead action: a dedicated IVR path for 'I received an alert' with the authority to lift at first contact; measure transfers per alert call.

open: The alert itself: which purchase, when it was sent, and to which number
The card's status: restricted or open
The contact history, so you can see how many times they have been transferred
What your desk can lift on its own and what has to go to the fraud team. Confirm in your systems.
know: This call has to be the one that ends the loop. Transfer only if procedure leaves no choice, and then do it warm: reach the colleague first, brief them, introduce the client by name.
The alert may be the scam. A real alert asks for a yes or a no. It never asks for a link, a code or a PIN.
Never ask for a one-time code yourself.
They have told this story more than once. Read the notes and say back what you know before you ask anything.

confirm: Say what happened to the charge: confirmed as theirs, or blocked and reported
Say what state the card is in now and whether they can use it
Read back the number the alerts now go to
lines: "That purchase is confirmed as yours and the card is working again. Is that what you needed when you first answered our text?"
"Is there anything left over from the earlier calls that nobody dealt with?"

ask: "When our text arrived, what did it ask you to do?"
"Is this the number you want alerts sent to?"
"Has anyone ever called you saying they were from the bank and asked for a code?"

options.do: Show how to answer an alert
options.why: One reply clears a real purchase in seconds. The trade-off: they need the phone on them when they shop.

options.do: Teach the tell of a fake alert
options.why: A real one asks yes or no. Anything that asks for a link, a code or a PIN is not the bank. The trade-off: none.

options.do: Set the alert number
options.why: The alert lands where they will see it. The trade-off: it has to be kept current.

options.do: Call the number on the back of the card
options.why: They reach the bank on a number they trust, not one from a message. The trade-off: none.

callAdvice.notNow: Any product or offer. They came to answer the bank's own question and have already lost time to transfers.

recap: What the alert was about and what was decided
The state of the card now
How to answer the next alert
An apology for the transfers, said once and plainly
lines: "To recap: the alert was about the purchase at [merchant], you confirmed it is yours, and the card is clear. Next time, a one-word reply to the text does all of this."
"I am sorry it took this many calls to answer one text. It should have been simpler."
"Is there anything else I can help you with today? Thank you for sticking with it."

depths.agent: Act on the alert at first contact; never transfer; teach the tell.
depths.specialist: Own the alert-to-restriction rules: which alerts auto-restrict, which the desk can lift, which need fraud.
depths.lead: Transfers per alert call and time-to-lift are the two numbers; both are routing decisions you control.

breakdowns.title: Replacement or renewal card slow, missing, or sent to the wrong address
breakdowns.surfaceRequest: "Where is my card?" On the second or third contact: "Your colleague said it would be here by Tuesday."
breakdowns.underlyingJob: Have a working card before the old one dies or the trip starts, and keep the bills it pays from bouncing. On repeat contact the job becomes: be believed and get a date someone keeps.
breakdowns.emotionalRead: Anxiety that becomes anger with each contact; often expressed as exhaustion ("I'm not angry at you, I'm just done"). Tell: counts the contacts, quotes the broken promise verbatim.
breakdowns.psychologicalNeeds: Control and fairness (I did everything right), being believed (the previous person said a date), competence of the institution.
riskFlags: Address updated after the card was issued: the first card went to the old address by design, and that is a process gap worth naming
Pre-authorised payments on the old number: some updated by the Account Updater, some not; fees may have been charged by merchants
Credits or points on the cancelled account that did not migrate (the FCAC fine pattern)
Third contact or more without a complaint code: it is a complaint, and the clock started at the first expression of dissatisfaction
A prior advisor's unsupportable promise: own it, do not repeat it
breakdowns.engage: "Fourth contact, a card to the wrong address, a promise for Tuesday that was not kept, and two payments bounced with a fee. I am not going to give you another wait. Here is what happens on this call."
diagnose: Which address is on file now, and since when? (explains the first mis-delivery)
Which payments are on the old number, and which have failed? (scope the damage)
Is there a refund or credit on the cancelled account? (check migration)
Do you need a card in three days or ten? (emergency versus standard)
breakdowns.resolve: Order the emergency replacement to the confirmed address with tracking; move any stranded refund or credit to the new account now; list the PAPs and tell them which updated and which they must change; address the merchant fee (reverse where policy allows, otherwise the path); log the complaint with the correct start date and explain the 56-day period and OBSI route; written confirmation with the dates. Set up a wallet for the gap.

sayThisNotThis.say: "The card went to the old address because the address change landed a day after it was issued; that is our gap to fix, not yours."
sayThisNotThis.not: "The card was sent to the address on file."
sayThisNotThis.why: Names the mechanism and takes the gap.

sayThisNotThis.say: "I am ordering the emergency card now; it arrives in three business days or less, and I am sending you the tracking."
sayThisNotThis.why: The standard window is the wrong answer on a fourth contact.

sayThisNotThis.say: "I have logged this as a complaint, dated from the 26th when you first raised it, and you will have our written answer within 56 days of that."
sayThisNotThis.not: "I'll make a note on your file."
sayThisNotThis.why: A note is not a complaint; the regulator has said so.

breakdowns.afterCall: Note: emergency replacement ordered, tracking sent; refund [amount] transferred to new account; PAP list with status; merchant fee action; complaint logged with start date [first contact]; Designated Employee referral if unresolved; written acknowledgement sent.
breakdowns.preventAndFeedBack: Drivers: address changes not applied to in-flight card orders; stranded credits on migration; advisors promising dates standard delivery cannot keep. Lead action: a hold-and-reissue check when an address changes within 10 days of issue; a migration checklist that includes credits; coaching on promises.

open: The card order history: what was ordered, when, by which delivery method, and to which address
The address on file now and the date it last changed
Notes from every earlier contact, including any date a colleague gave
Recurring payments tied to the old card number, and any that have failed
Credits, refunds or points sitting on the closed card number
know: Count the contacts before you greet them. On a third or fourth contact the standard wait is the wrong answer.
Own an earlier promise that was not kept. Do not repeat it, and do not blame the colleague.
Repeated dissatisfaction is a complaint, and its clock runs from the first time they raised it. The timelines are in Policy for this issue. Confirm in your systems.
Only give a date the delivery method can keep.

confirm: Read back the delivery address, slowly if it was wrong before
Give the delivery method, the date range and how the tracking will reach them. Confirm the range in your systems.
Confirm which payments moved to the new number on their own and which they must change
lines: "The new card is going to [address], and you will have the tracking by message today. Is that the right address?"
"Apart from the card itself, is anything still stuck: a payment, a refund, a fee?"

ask: "Which payments come off this card each month?"
"Is there a date you need the card by, like a trip or a renewal?"
"How would you like us to confirm things with you: text, email or mail?"

options.do: Go through the recurring payments together
options.why: No bounced bill and no merchant fee. The trade-off: a few more minutes on this call.

options.do: Explain the two delivery options

options.why: They may be able to pay before the plastic arrives. The trade-off: not every card can be added before it is activated, so check before you say it. Confirm in your systems.

options.do: Confirm the address and contact details on everything they hold
options.why: The next card goes to the right door. The trade-off: none.

callAdvice.notNow: A different card, an upgrade or any product. They are on a repeat contact and a complaint is open.

breakdowns.title: Dispute for goods not delivered or merchant failure
breakdowns.surfaceRequest: "I paid, it never came, the merchant will not answer. Get my money back."
breakdowns.underlyingJob: Recover money from a merchant who did not deliver, with a date they can rely on and a sense that someone is actually investigating.
breakdowns.emotionalRead: Anger with a strong unheard quality; the caller has often already been bounced between the merchant, a payment processor and the bank. Tell: "nobody will give me a straight answer."
breakdowns.psychologicalNeeds: Fairness and being heard; control (a date, a reference, a person).
riskFlags: Authorised purchases are merchant disputes, not fraud: do not promise zero-liability treatment
Window: 120 days from the transaction or expected delivery (540-day ceiling); check the dates before promising anything
Evidence decides it: order confirmation, delivery promise, merchant correspondence
A date given and kept is the single most praised behaviour in the corpus; a date given and missed is the single most cursed
breakdowns.engage: "You paid, it never arrived, and you have been sent around. This is a merchant dispute and there is a real process with stages. I will tell you what each stage is and what I need from you, and you will have a reference and a written summary before we hang up."
diagnose: When was the transaction, and when were the goods due? (window check)
What have you already done with the merchant, and what do you have in writing?
What evidence exists: order confirmation, tracking, emails, photos?
breakdowns.resolve: If the merchant has not been contacted: explain why that step is required and what to send, with a date to come back. If it has: open the dispute, state the evidence attached, explain the network stages and realistic ranges (30 to 45 days straightforward, 60 to 90 contested, longer in arbitration) rather than a single date, give the reference, and promise the written summary. Temporary credit per policy, with the honest caveat that it can reverse if the merchant provides evidence.

sayThisNotThis.say: "Here is the reference, here are the stages, and you will hear from us in writing at each one."
sayThisNotThis.why: Stages and a reference are what being heard looks like.

sayThisNotThis.say: "The merchant step is the network's requirement, and it is also the fastest route to your money if they respond; send them this exact wording."
sayThisNotThis.not: "You have to contact the merchant first."
sayThisNotThis.why: Same requirement, explained as a route rather than a wall.

sayThisNotThis.say: "A temporary credit is likely within a couple of business days, and I want to be straight that it can reverse if the merchant proves delivery."
sayThisNotThis.why: Honest about reversibility; prevents the worse call later.

breakdowns.afterCall: Note: dispute reference, reason code, evidence attached, window dates, what the client was told about stages and reversibility, written summary sent, follow-up date owned by you.
breakdowns.preventAndFeedBack: Drivers: clients unsure what evidence is needed; no written summary at intake. Lead action: an evidence checklist in the app dispute flow; a written-summary macro at intake; measure disputes reopened for missing evidence.

open: The transaction: date, amount, the merchant name as it shows on the statement, and whether it has posted
The dispute window for that date (Policy for this issue). Check it before you promise anything, and confirm in your systems.
Any earlier dispute or note on the same charge

Give stages, not a single date. A date you miss costs more than a range you keep.
A temporary credit can reverse if the merchant proves delivery. Say so up front.
They have usually been bounced between the merchant and others already. Being heard comes first.

options.do: Keep the proof for every online order
options.why: The confirmation, the promised date and any messages decide a dispute. The trade-off: a folder to keep.

options.do: Raise a problem early
options.why: The dispute window is counted in days from the purchase or the promised delivery. The trade-off: chasing the merchant sooner than feels polite.

options.do: Turn on transaction alerts
options.why: A repeat charge from the same merchant is seen the day it happens. The trade-off: more messages.

options.do: Check a new merchant before paying
options.why: Reviews and a real address cut the risk. The trade-off: a few minutes before each first order.

callAdvice.notNow: Purchase protection add-ons, a different card or any product while the money is still missing and they feel unheard.
